title: Connected talk
verifiedBy: Claude Opus 5 — LLM review, authorised by repo owner

rules.text: A turn is two or three short sentences, not one long one. Korean packs a lot into few words, so the natural shape of a spoken turn is a statement, then another statement, then perhaps a question — each of them finishing with its own verb.

Korean joins ideas in two different places. A CONNECTOR starts a new sentence: geurigo ('and'), geunde ('but'), geuraeseo ('so'). An ENDING joins clauses inside one sentence: -go ('and then') on the verb stem, and M9's -aseo ('because'). Same relationships, two grammatical places, and choosing the wrong one is what makes a turn read as translated.

Say the subject once at most, and usually not at all. Once a turn is about you, every following sentence leaves you out. Repeating jeo-neun in each sentence is grammatical and it is the clearest sign of an English speaker — it reads as 'as for ME' every time, as if you kept correcting somebody.

-go on a verb stem strings two actions in the order they happen: bap meokgo cha masyeoyo, 'I eat and then drink tea'. Only the LAST verb carries the tense and the politeness — the first one stays in its bare -go shape.

The style has to hold across the whole turn. Every verb ends in -yo, and the only exceptions in this course are the two frozen phrases from M2. One slip into a different style inside a turn is audible in a way that a single odd sentence is not.

geunde is the everyday 'but' — the clipped form of geureonde — and it does two jobs: it contrasts (this, but that) and it can change the subject gently ('by the way'). hajiman is the plain written contrast; you will read it more often than hear it. All three begin a new sentence.

words.note: 'Hello', from M2 — the opening of any turn.
'My', from M1.
'Name', from M1.
A man's given name, from M1.

sentences.trap: Two sentences and no connector. English would often join them — 'hello, my name is Minsu' — and Korean simply stops after the greeting and starts again, which is why the pause is worth making.
sentences.sound: an-nyung-ha-SE-yo. jeh ee-RUM-un MIN-soo-yeh-yo. A real full stop between them: the greeting falls, then the introduction starts fresh.

variations.display: Annyeonghaseyo. Jeo-neun Minsu-yeyo.
variations.script: 안녕하세요. 저는 민수예요.
variations.cue: Hello. I am Minsu.
variations.changed: the shorter introduction, with the person as the topic

variations.display: Annyeonghaseyo. Oraenmanieyo.
variations.script: 안녕하세요. 오랜만이에요.
variations.cue: Hello. It has been a long time.
variations.changed: the greeting and the remark that often follows it

variations.display: Annyeonghaseyo. Je ireum-eun Yuna-yeyo.
variations.script: 안녕하세요. 제 이름은 유나예요.
variations.cue: Hello. My name is Yuna.
variations.changed: a different name

mistake.why: A connector has been used to glue a greeting to an introduction. geurigo joins two statements; a greeting is not a statement, and nothing needs to join them.

sentences.usage: Opening any conversation with somebody new.
sentences.mnemonic: Greet, stop, then say who you are.

sentences.cue: I am a student. And I study Korean.

words.note: 'I', from M1 — and this module is where you learn to stop saying it. Once a turn is about you, every sentence after the first leaves it out.
'Student', from M1.
'And', joining one whole sentence to the next. It starts the second sentence rather than sitting between two things — Korean does not use it the way English uses 'and' inside a list of nouns.
'Korean', the language, from M1.
'Learn', from M3.

sentences.trap: The second sentence has no subject, and that is the whole lesson of this module. The turn is already about you; saying jeo-neun again would read as if you were distinguishing yourself from somebody else.
sentences.sound: juh-nun HAK-ssaeng-ee-eh-yo. gu-RI-go han-GOONG-ma-rul BAE-wuh-yo. geurigo is three light beats and starts the second sentence cleanly.

variations.display: Jeo-neun haksaeng-ieyo. Geurigo maeil gongbuhaeyo.
variations.script: 저는 학생이에요. 그리고 매일 공부해요.
variations.cue: I am a student. And I study every day.
variations.changed: a different second half

variations.display: Jeo-neun haksaeng-ieyo. Geunde oneul-eun an bappayo.
variations.script: 저는 학생이에요. 근데 오늘은 안 바빠요.
variations.cue: I'm a student. But today I'm not busy.
variations.changed: a contrast instead of an addition

variations.display: Haksaeng-ieyo. Geurigo hangungmal-eul baewoyo.
variations.script: 학생이에요. 그리고 한국말을 배워요.
variations.cue: I am a student. And I study Korean.
variations.changed: the subject dropped from the first sentence too, which is what a Korean speaker would do in reply to a question

mistake.display: Jeo-neun haksaeng-ieyo. Geurigo jeo-neun hangungmal-eul baewoyo.
mistake.script: 저는 학생이에요. 그리고 저는 한국말을 배워요.
mistake.why: The subject has been repeated in the second sentence. It is grammatical and it is the anglophone tell — the turn is already about you, so the second jeo-neun reads as a correction.

sentences.usage: Saying two things about yourself in a row.
sentences.mnemonic: Name yourself once, then let the turn remember.

sentences.display: Oneul-eun bappayo. Geunde naeil-eun an bappayo.
sentences.script: 오늘은 바빠요. 근데 내일은 안 바빠요.
sentences.cue: I am busy today. But tomorrow I am not.
sentences.literal: today-topic is-busy. but tomorrow-topic not is-busy

words.note: 'Today', from M4.
'Is busy', from M9 — a describing word, and so a verb.
'But', as it is said: geunde is the everyday clipping of geureonde, and hajiman is the same contrast in writing and careful speech. All three begin a new sentence.
'Tomorrow', from M6.
'Not', from M3, still immediately in front of the verb.

sentences.trap: The topic marker on both days is what makes the contrast work. Without it the two sentences are simply two facts; with it they are set against each other, which is exactly the job geunde is doing.
sentences.sound: O-neu-run BA-ppa-yo. GUN-de NAE-i-run an BA-ppa-yo. Both time words link into their markers — o-neu-run, nae-i-run — and geunde is two light beats that start the second sentence.

variations.display: Oneul-eun bappayo. Geunde naeil-eun gal geoyeyo.
variations.script: 오늘은 바빠요. 근데 내일은 갈 거예요.
variations.cue: I'm busy today. But tomorrow I'll go.
variations.changed: a different contrast, in the future

variations.display: Oneul-eun an bappayo. Geurigo naeil-eun an bappayo.
variations.script: 오늘은 안 바빠요. 그리고 내일은 안 바빠요.
variations.cue: I'm not busy today. And I'm not busy tomorrow.
variations.changed: addition rather than contrast

variations.display: Oneul-eun bappayo. Geunde jip-e an gayo.
variations.script: 오늘은 바빠요. 근데 집에 안 가요.
variations.cue: I'm busy today. But I'm not going home.
variations.changed: a different pair of facts under the same contrast

mistake.display: Oneul-eun bappayo geunde naeil-eun an bappayo.
mistake.script: 오늘은 바빠요 근데 내일은 안 바빠요.
mistake.why: The two sentences have been run together with no stop. geunde begins a sentence; to join clauses inside one sentence you need an ending on the verb, not a connector.

sentences.mnemonic: Mark both days, then set them against each other.

sentences.cue: I eat and then drink tea.

words.note: 'A meal', from M3 — bare, as it is said.
'Eat', from M3 — and meokgo is doing a new job here. In M3 it sat in front of sipeoyo; on its own it joins one clause to the next, so bap meokgo cha masyeoyo is 'I eat and then drink tea'.
'Tea', from M1.
'Drink', from M3 — and masigo is its joining shape, built the same way as meokgo.

sentences.trap: meokgo is the same shape you learned in front of sipeoyo, doing a different job. On its own it means 'and then', and the first verb stays bare — it carries no tense and no -yo, because the last verb carries both for the whole sentence.
sentences.sound: bap MUK-go cha ma-SHUH-yo. There is no pause after meokgo: the two halves are one sentence, and running them together is what tells the listener so.

variations.display: Bap meokgo hakgyo-e gayo.
variations.script: 밥 먹고 학교에 가요.
variations.cue: I eat and then go to school.
variations.changed: a different second action

variations.display: Bap meokgo cha masyeosseoyo.
variations.script: 밥 먹고 차 마셨어요.
variations.cue: I ate and then drank tea.
variations.changed: the past — and only the last verb changes

variations.display: Cha masigo gongbuhaeyo.
variations.script: 차 마시고 공부해요.
variations.cue: I drink tea and then study.
variations.changed: the other verb wearing -go this time

mistake.why: The ending has been put on the finished -yo form. -go goes on the STEM: meokgo, exactly as it did in M3's meokgo sipeoyo.

sentences.usage: Describing two things you do in order.
sentences.mnemonic: The first verb waits bare; the last one carries the tense.

sentences.display: Jip-e keopi-ga eopseoyo. Geuraeseo hakgyo-eseo masyeoyo.
sentences.script: 집에 커피가 없어요. 그래서 학교에서 마셔요.
sentences.cue: There is no coffee at home. So I drink it at school.
sentences.literal: home-at coffee-subject does-not-exist. so school-at drink

words.note: 'Home', from M7.
The point marker, from M4 and M7 — a time or a place.
'Coffee', from M1.
'There is not', from M3.
'So', from M9 — the connector that gives a reason for what follows.
'School', from M7 — with -e for being or going there and -eseo for doing something there.
The action-place marker, from M7.
'Drink', from M3 — and masigo is its joining shape, built the same way as meokgo.

sentences.trap: Both place markers appear in one turn and each is doing its own job: -e for where the coffee is not, -eseo for where the drinking happens. This is M7's split in the wild, and getting it right across two sentences is the test.
sentences.sound: JI-be KUH-pee-ga UP-suh-yo. gu-RAE-suh HAK-gyo-e-suh ma-SHUH-yo. The two markers are a beat apart in the same turn, which makes the length difference easy to hear.

variations.display: Jip-e cha-ga eopseoyo. Geuraeseo hakgyo-eseo masyeoyo.
variations.script: 집에 차가 없어요. 그래서 학교에서 마셔요.
variations.cue: There is no tea at home. So I drink it at school.
variations.changed: a different thing missing

variations.display: Jip-e keopi-ga eopseoyo. Geunde hakgyo-e isseoyo.
variations.script: 집에 커피가 없어요. 근데 학교에 있어요.
variations.cue: There's no coffee at home. But there is at school.
variations.changed: a contrast, and existence at both ends so both places take -e

variations.display: Jip-e keopi-ga eopseoseo hakgyo-eseo masyeoyo.
variations.script: 집에 커피가 없어서 학교에서 마셔요.
variations.cue: Because there is no coffee at home, I drink it at school.
variations.changed: the same turn as one sentence, with M9's ending instead of the connector

mistake.display: Jip-eseo keopi-ga eopseoyo. Geuraeseo hakgyo-e masyeoyo.
mistake.script: 집에서 커피가 없어요. 그래서 학교에 마셔요.
mistake.why: Both markers have been swapped. Nothing happens at the house — the coffee simply is not there, so -e — and the drinking does happen at school, so -eseo.

sentences.usage: Explaining a small habit and its reason.
sentences.mnemonic: One turn, two places, two different markers.

sentences.display: Eoje jal jasseoyo. Geuraeseo oneul an pigonhaeyo.
sentences.script: 어제 잘 잤어요. 그래서 오늘 안 피곤해요.
sentences.cue: I slept well yesterday. So I'm not tired today.
sentences.literal: yesterday well slept. so today not is-tired

words.note: 'Yesterday', from M5, still taking no marker.
'Well', from M2, in front of the verb it describes.
'Sleep', from M4, with its past from M5.
'So', from M9 — the connector that gives a reason for what follows.
'Today', from M4.
'Not', from M3, still immediately in front of the verb.
'Is tired', from M9 — a describing word, and so a verb.

sentences.trap: Two sentences, two tenses: the first is about yesterday and carries the past; the second is about today and stays in the present. Nothing has to be matched up — each sentence pays its own tense, and the eoje at the start covers only its own sentence.
sentences.sound: UH-je jal JA-ssuh-yo. gu-RAE-suh O-neul an pee-gon-HAE-yo. The first sentence falls, then geuraeseo starts the second; an leans onto pigonhaeyo as always.

variations.display: Eoje jal jasseoyo. Geurigo oneul-eun bappayo.
variations.script: 어제 잘 잤어요. 그리고 오늘은 바빠요.
variations.cue: I slept well yesterday. And today I'm busy.
variations.changed: an addition instead of a consequence, and the second sentence in the present again

variations.display: Eoje an jasseoyo. Geuraeseo pigonhaeyo.
variations.script: 어제 안 잤어요. 그래서 피곤해요.
variations.cue: I didn't sleep yesterday. So I'm tired.
variations.changed: both halves the other way round — no sleep, and tired

variations.display: Eoje jal jasseoyo. Geunde oneul pigonhaeyo.
variations.script: 어제 잘 잤어요. 근데 오늘 피곤해요.
variations.cue: I slept well yesterday. But I'm tired today.
variations.changed: a contrast instead of a consequence

mistake.display: Eoje jal jasseoyo. Geuraeseo oneul an pigonhaesseoyo.
mistake.script: 어제 잘 잤어요. 그래서 오늘 안 피곤했어요.
mistake.why: The second sentence has been dragged into the past, as if the eoje at the start of the turn covered both. Today is now, so its verb stays in the present.

sentences.usage: Telling somebody how you slept and how you feel.
sentences.mnemonic: Every sentence pays its own tense.

sentences.display: Wae hakgyo-e an gayo? Bappaseo an gayo.
sentences.script: 왜 학교에 안 가요? 바빠서 안 가요.
sentences.cue: Why aren't you going to school? Because I am busy.
sentences.literal: why school-to not go? busy-because not go

words.note: 'Why', from M9 — in place, with the voice asking.
'School', from M7 — with -e for being or going there and -eseo for doing something there.
The point marker, from M4 and M7 — a time or a place.
'Not', from M3, still immediately in front of the verb.
'Go', from M6.
'Is busy', from M9 — a describing word, and so a verb.
The 'because' ending, from M9 — on the stem of the reason, and the reason comes first.

sentences.trap: The answer repeats the verb rather than replacing it with a short 'because I'm busy'. Korean answers in the shape of the question, and the repeated an gayo is what makes it a real reply rather than a fragment.
sentences.sound: WAE HAK-gyo-e an GA-yo, rising. BA-ppa-suh an GA-yo, falling. The question lifts and the answer drops, and the two halves are otherwise built the same way.

variations.display: Wae hakgyo-e an gayo? Bappaseo jip-e isseoyo.
variations.script: 왜 학교에 안 가요? 바빠서 집에 있어요.
variations.cue: Why aren't you going to school? I am at home because I am busy.
variations.changed: an answer that adds where you are instead

variations.display: Wae hangungmal-eul baewoyo? Hanguk-e gal geoyeyo.
variations.script: 왜 한국말을 배워요? 한국에 갈 거예요.
variations.cue: Why do you study Korean? I am going to go to Korea.
variations.changed: an answer with no because-ending at all — the reason is left implied

variations.display: Wae bappayo? Il-i manaseo bappayo.
variations.script: 왜 바빠요? 일이 많아서 바빠요.
variations.cue: Why are you busy? I have a lot of work.
variations.changed: the same pair with a describing verb in both halves

mistake.display: Wae hakgyo-e an gayo? Bappayo geuraeseo.
mistake.script: 왜 학교에 안 가요? 바빠요 그래서.
mistake.why: The connector has been put at the end of the answer, where English can put 'so'. geuraeseo begins a sentence, and nothing follows a Korean verb.

sentences.usage: Asking and answering about a reason.
sentences.mnemonic: Answer in the shape of the question.

sentences.display: Cha-reul joahaeyo. Geunde oneul-eun keopi-reul masyeoyo.
sentences.script: 차를 좋아해요. 근데 오늘은 커피를 마셔요.
sentences.cue: I like tea. But today I am drinking coffee.
sentences.literal: tea-object like. but today-topic coffee-object drink

words.note: 'Tea', from M1.
'Like', from M1 — a verb taking an object with -eul/-reul.
'But', as it is said: geunde is the everyday clipping of geureonde, and hajiman is the same contrast in writing and careful speech. All three begin a new sentence.
'Today', from M4.
'Coffee', from M1.
'Drink', from M3 — and masigo is its joining shape, built the same way as meokgo.

sentences.trap: joahaeyo takes an object with -reul, and the contrast in the second sentence is carried by the topic marker on oneul. Two different markers, two different jobs, and neither can do the other's.
sentences.sound: CHA-rul jo-ah-HAE-yo. GUN-de O-neu-run KUH-pee-rul ma-SHUH-yo. The h in joahaeyo is silent again, and the whole first sentence is three beats.

variations.display: Keopi-reul joahaeyo. Geunde oneul-eun cha-reul masyeoyo.
variations.script: 커피를 좋아해요. 근데 오늘은 차를 마셔요.
variations.cue: I like coffee. But today I'm drinking tea.
variations.changed: the two halves swapped

variations.display: Cha-reul joahaeyo. Geurigo maeil masyeoyo.
variations.script: 차를 좋아해요. 그리고 매일 마셔요.
variations.cue: I like tea. And I drink it every day.
variations.changed: addition rather than contrast

variations.display: Cha-ga joayo. Geunde oneul-eun keopi-reul masyeoyo.
variations.script: 차가 좋아요. 근데 오늘은 커피를 마셔요.
variations.cue: Tea is good. But today I'm drinking coffee.
variations.changed: M9's describing verb in the first half, with -ga instead of -reul

mistake.display: Cha-ga joahaeyo. Geunde oneul-eun keopi-reul masyeoyo.
mistake.script: 차가 좋아해요. 근데 오늘은 커피를 마셔요.
mistake.why: The subject marker has been used with joahaeyo. That verb takes an OBJECT — cha-reul joahaeyo — and -ga belongs with joayo, the describing verb that says the tea itself is good.

sentences.usage: Saying what you usually like and what you are doing instead.
sentences.mnemonic: Liking takes an object; being good takes a subject.

sentences.display: Naeil hanguk-e gal geoyeyo. Geurigo hangungmal-eul baeul geoyeyo.
sentences.script: 내일 한국에 갈 거예요. 그리고 한국말을 배울 거예요.
sentences.cue: I will go to Korea tomorrow. And I will study Korean.
sentences.literal: tomorrow Korea-to go-thing-is. and Korean-object learn-thing-is

words.note: 'Tomorrow', from M6.
'Korea', from M1.
The point marker, from M4 and M7 — a time or a place.
'Go', from M6.
The future's second half, from M6.
'And', joining one whole sentence to the next. It starts the second sentence rather than sitting between two things — Korean does not use it the way English uses 'and' inside a list of nouns.
'Korean', the language, from M1.
'Learn', from M3.

sentences.trap: Both halves are in the future and both build it the same way, but the verb shapes differ — gal after a vowel-final stem, baeul after a consonant. It is the rule from M6 running twice in one turn.
sentences.sound: NAE-il HAN-goo-ge gal GUH-ye-yo. gu-RI-go han-GOONG-ma-rul BAE-ul GUH-ye-yo. Two futures in a row, and the geoyeyo at the end of each is what closes the sentence.

variations.display: Naeil hanguk-e gayo. Geurigo hangungmal-eul baewoyo.
variations.script: 내일 한국에 가요. 그리고 한국말을 배워요.
variations.cue: I am going to Korea tomorrow. And I am studying Korean.
variations.changed: the plain present doing the future's job in both halves

variations.display: Naeil hanguk-e gal geoyeyo. Geunde hangungmal-eul an baeul geoyeyo.
variations.script: 내일 한국에 갈 거예요. 근데 한국말을 안 배울 거예요.
variations.cue: I'm going to Korea tomorrow. But I won't learn Korean.
variations.changed: a contrast, with the second half negated

variations.display: Hanguk-e gal geoyeyo. Geuraeseo hangungmal-eul baewoyo.
variations.script: 한국에 갈 거예요. 그래서 한국말을 배워요.
variations.cue: I will go to Korea. So I am studying Korean.
variations.changed: the reason connector from M9, which changes what the two sentences are to each other

mistake.display: Naeil hanguk-e gal geoyeyo geurigo hangungmal-eul baeul geoyeyo.
mistake.script: 내일 한국에 갈 거예요 그리고 한국말을 배울 거예요.
mistake.why: No stop between the sentences. A connector needs one in front of it; without the stop you have one sentence with two verbs in it, which Korean does not allow.

sentences.usage: Laying out a plan with two parts.
sentences.mnemonic: Two futures, two sentences, one connector between them.

sentences.cue: It has been a long time. Have you been well?

words.cue: it has been a long time
words.note: 'It has been a while', from M2.
'Well', from M2, in front of the verb it describes.
'Get by', from M2, in its past shape jinaesseoyo — asking how the stretch since you last met went. A single day is asked about with M5's bonaesseoyo.

sentences.trap: The past here asks about the stretch of time since you last met, not about yesterday — a single day is asked about with M5's bonaesseoyo. jal jinaeseyo? asks about life now; this asks how the gap went, which is exactly why it follows oraenmanieyo.
sentences.sound: o-raen-ma-NEE-eh-yo. jal ji-NAE-ssuh-yo, rising at the end. The first sentence falls and the second lifts — two sentences, two shapes, one turn.

variations.display: Oraenmanieyo. Jal jinaeseyo?
variations.script: 오랜만이에요. 잘 지내세요?
variations.cue: It has been a long time. Are you well?
variations.changed: the present, asking about how things are now

variations.display: Annyeonghaseyo. Oraenmanieyo.
variations.script: 안녕하세요. 오랜만이에요.
variations.cue: Hello. It has been a long time.
variations.changed: the greeting first, which is how the turn usually opens

variations.display: Oraenmanieyo. Jal jinaesseoyo.
variations.script: 오랜만이에요. 잘 지냈어요.
variations.cue: It has been a long time. I have been well.
variations.changed: said flat, the second sentence answers rather than asks

mistake.why: A connector has been put between a remark and a question. geurigo joins statements; a question after a remark simply follows it, with a stop in between.

sentences.usage: Meeting somebody after a long gap.
sentences.mnemonic: Remark, stop, question — and the voice does the asking.

comprehensionPool.cue: I am a student. And I study every day.

comprehensionPool.display: Oneul-eun bappayo. Geunde naeil-eun an bappayo.
comprehensionPool.script: 오늘은 바빠요. 근데 내일은 안 바빠요.
comprehensionPool.cue: I am busy today. But tomorrow I am not.
I eat and then go to school.
I did not sleep yesterday. So I am tired.
I like tea. And I drink it every day.
Why are you busy? I have a lot of work.

comprehensionPool.display: Jip-e keopi-ga eopseoyo. Geunde hakgyo-e isseoyo.
comprehensionPool.script: 집에 커피가 없어요. 근데 학교에 있어요.
comprehensionPool.cue: There is no coffee at home. But there is at school.

comprehensionPool.display: Naeil hanguk-e gal geoyeyo. Geurigo hangungmal-eul baeul geoyeyo.
